kf1.tip: Rank Dickens's father's imprisonment for debt, his blacking factory work and his wish to help poor children by how far each drove him to write the novella, a line each.
kf1.note: A strong answer sees these as a chain, not three separate facts. His father's imprisonment for debt is why twelve-year-old Charles was sent to the blacking factory. That childhood trauma shaped his lifelong passion for social justice. Most would rank his wish to help poor children first, because the 1843 report on children working in mines and factories was the direct trigger. The trap is listing the three facts with no link between them.

kf2.tip: Imagine Dickens had set A Christmas Carol in midsummer instead of at Christmas. Write two things his message about social responsibility would lose.
kf2.note: A strong answer weighs what Christmas already did for Dickens. Readers were already thinking about generosity, family and goodwill, so his call to help the poor met them halfway. Christmas was also going mainstream, with cards, crackers and trees newly introduced, so the season amplified his message. You might also note the title and the five staves present the book as a carol. The trap is listing surface losses like presents instead of what the message loses.

cs1.tip: Trace the steps from Thomas Malthus's famine warning to Scrooge's "decrease the surplus population", then name the weakest step in that reasoning and say why.
cs1.note: A strong chain has four steps. Malthus warned that unchecked population growth would outstrip food and bring famine. Some Victorians turned this into the view that reducing the population was desirable. They used that to justify not helping the poor. Scrooge echoes it with "decrease the surplus population". Most would name the second step as weakest, because a warning about disaster becomes a wish to see the poor gone. The trap is attacking Malthus's warning instead of that jump.
